paragraphs: Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model. It's based on Qwen3.8-27B and takes up just 5.9 GB of memory, same as its predecessor. That's possible because of ternary quantization, where each weight can only be one of three values (−1, 0, or +1) instead of the usual 16-bit storage. At full precision, a model this size would need about 54 GB.

Bonsai 2.5 is designed to perform more reliably on agentic tasks that involve long chains of tool calls. It needs fewer passes and tokens than Bonsai 2, and it's less likely to get stuck in loops or spiral into drawn-out reasoning phases.

The benchmark numbers reflect the improvement. On SWE-bench Verified, the score jumps from 60.8 to 75.6 percent. The full Qwen model hits 80.6. On AppWorld, an agent benchmark, Bonsai leaps from 51.2 to 90.5, landing just behind the base model. On LiveCodeBench v6, the new version scores slightly lower than its predecessor.

On an RTX 4090, the model generates about 204 tokens per second using multi-token prediction. The weights are available under an Apache 2.0 license and run via llama.cpp on Nvidia and Intel GPUs, as well as through MLX on Mac, iPhone, and iPad. PrismML grew out of a research team at Caltech and is backed by Khosla Ventures, Google, and Samsung, among others. The company first introduced Bonsai 27B in July, built on an older Qwen model. Its smallest variant needed less than 4 GB of memory, small enough to run directly on an iPhone.

top_three.title_en: Asia Data Centers Sound Out US Clients to Replace China Demand

inline_images.caption: New US AI chip rules against China threaten Southeast Asia’s data centers

top_three.author: Bloomberg
top_three.content_snippet:
Washington has spent years stopping advanced AI chips from physically reaching China. It turns out the chips never had to travel at all.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department issued a rule aimed at Chinese companies that tap high-end AI hardware sitting in data centers outside China. The move lands hardest on Southeast Asia, a region that has been building server farms at a brisk clip.

The rule comes from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS. It is an interim final
top_three.summary_en: The US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule, effective around November 16, 2026, targeting remote access to high-end AI compute by Chinese entities at non-US data centers. Facilities providing significant compute, exceeding 12 million aggregate TPP, are required to implement enhanced due diligence and obtain licenses, facing potential trade restrictions for non-compliance.
paragraphs: Washington has spent years stopping advanced AI chips from physically reaching China. It turns out the chips never had to travel at all.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department issued a rule aimed at Chinese companies that tap high-end AI hardware sitting in data centers outside China. The move lands hardest on Southeast Asia, a region that has been building server farms at a brisk clip.
The rule comes from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS. It is an interim final rule, with an effective date of approximately November 16, 2026.
Its core target is remote access. A Chinese firm does not need to own an Nvidia or AMD chip to use one. It can simply rent compute from a facility abroad and run its workloads over the internet.

The rule also reaches data centers directly. Any facility providing significant compute to Chinese entities needs a license and must carry out enhanced due diligence once it crosses a threshold of over 12 million aggregate TPP.
Operators get a 90-day compliance window after the rule takes effect. Those that miss it may face future restrictions.
There is one notable carve-out. US-headquartered operators are exempt from certain licensing requirements, though they must submit monthly compliance reports.

The rule is largely a response to the scandal around Nvidia and Megaspeed, a data center operator. Megaspeed spent at least $4.6 billion on Nvidia servers between 2023 and 2025.

The controversy centers on allegations that chips were diverted and that major Chinese clients, including Alibaba, gained remote access to compute. Those are allegations, not findings, but they were enough to push regulators into action.
Markets responded quickly. Shares of Southeast Asian companies linked to data centers fell after the announcement, with some dropping by as much as 20%.

top_three.title: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Trump’s Demands to Another Chips CEO
top_three.title_en: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Trump’s Demands to Another Chips CEO
top_three.author: Noah Shachtman
top_three.summary_en:
The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms o
paragraphs: The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”

Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”

President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”

Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

“It's just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what's best for the company in the short or long term, what's best for shareholders, but what's best for politics and what the government is demanding.”

“That's not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you're talking about the world's most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that's a huge problem.”
Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

topic_focus.summary_zh: 在硅谷投资界游说与特朗普政府直接干预下，深陷安全调查的黄仁勋重回英伟达掌舵。此事件引发了关于AI算力巨头是否已成为“大到无法监管”的质疑，美国情报部门正重点调查其关联公司的芯片出口流向。
topic_focus.summary_en: Following intense lobbying and direct intervention by the Trump administration, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia CEO despite security probes. This shift triggers debates over whether the chip giant has become 'too big to police,' with intelligence officials scrutinizing its export compliance and connections to controversial shell companies.

perspective_pro.speaker_zh: 英伟达董事会及华尔街分析师
perspective_pro.speaker_en: Nvidia Board and Wall Street Analysts
perspective_pro.point_zh: 英伟达在AI算力领域处于不可替代的核心地位，黄仁勋的回归能确保核心战略的连续性，维护美国在全球AI算力竞赛中的绝对领先优势。
perspective_pro.point_en: Nvidia holds an irreplaceable position in AI compute. Huang’s return ensures strategic continuity, preserving the U.S. lead in the global AI race against foreign rivals.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: 地缘政治分析师与合规专家
perspective_con.point_zh: 该行为开了政商干预企业合规的恶劣先例。当CEO拥有“总统豁免权”光环时，出口管制规则将形同虚设，导致国家安全边际被无限牺牲。
perspective_con.point_en: This sets a dangerous precedent for political interference in corporate compliance. When a CEO operates under the shield of 'presidential pardon,' export controls become moot, sacrificing national security for institutional convenience.

topic_focus.summary_zh: Meta正寻求将Muse AI代理植入亚马逊平台以获取实时购物数据，试图打通Instagram与电商的闭环。核心博弈在于搜索权重与用户行为数据所有权的归属，双方正争夺AI时代的消费者入口话语权。
topic_focus.summary_en: Meta is negotiating with Amazon to integrate its Muse AI agent for direct shopping on the platform. The deal aims to connect Instagram’s high-frequency user traffic with retail conversion. The core friction revolves around search visibility, data ownership, and control over the consumer interface in the post-search AI era.

perspective_pro.point_zh: 通过Muse AI将AI代理接入电商，能实现从种草到下单的无感转化，极大地缩短交易路径，提升流量货币化效率。
perspective_pro.point_en: Integrating Muse AI into retail platforms enables frictionless transactions from discovery to checkout, significantly shortening the customer journey and maximizing traffic monetization.

perspective_con.point_zh: 这本质上是Meta试图通过代理商蚕食电商平台的搜索入口。缺乏透明的利润分成模式，只会导致平台原生搜索算法被AI黑盒干扰。
perspective_con.point_en: This is essentially Meta trying to cannibalize the platform’s search dominance. Without transparent revenue-sharing, native search algorithms risk being undermined by AI black-box interference.

topic_focus.title_zh: 三星与SK海力士引入长江存储Xtacking堆叠技术
topic_focus.title_en: Samsung and SK Hynix Adopt YMTC’s Xtacking 3D NAND Technology
topic_focus.summary_zh: 存储巨头三星与SK海力士通过交叉许可协议，正式引入长江存储的Xtacking技术。这一罕见的技术博弈表明，在高性能3D NAND领域，尽管存在地缘封锁，行业领先的技术标准正在强制跨国企业进行反向技术妥协。
topic_focus.summary_en: Samsung and SK Hynix have reached cross-licensing deals to adopt YMTC’s Xtacking technology for 3D NAND flash. This rare strategic move signals that in the high-performance memory sector, industry-leading innovations are forcing global giants into reverse-licensing despite ongoing geopolitical containment efforts.

perspective_pro.point_zh: 技术进步是通用的，Xtacking通过更高效的架构显著降低了堆叠成本。商业利益与技术领先性往往高于地缘政治的简单阻隔。
perspective_pro.point_en: Technology is universal. Xtacking provides a more efficient architecture that drastically reduces stack costs. Commercial incentives and performance gains often outweigh the constraints of geopolitical barriers.

perspective_con.point_zh: 这种引入行为极易引发针对核心IP的审查。在当前贸易战语境下，依赖对手方的专利技术可能导致未来被纳入新的制裁清单风险。
perspective_con.point_en: Adopting this tech triggers significant regulatory scrutiny. In the current trade war context, relying on a competitor's IP risks pulling companies into new, unpredictable sanctions lists.

news.author: Jonathan Kemper

paragraphs: Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model. It's based on Qwen3.8-27B and takes up just 5.9 GB of memory, same as its predecessor. That's possible because of ternary quantization, where each weight can only be one of three values (−1, 0, or +1) instead of the usual 16-bit storage. At full precision, a model this size would need about 54 GB.

Bonsai 2.5 is designed to perform more reliably on agentic tasks that involve long chains of tool calls. It needs fewer passes and tokens than Bonsai 2, and it's less likely to get stuck in loops or spiral into drawn-out reasoning phases.

The benchmark numbers reflect the improvement. On SWE-bench Verified, the score jumps from 60.8 to 75.6 percent. The full Qwen model hits 80.6. On AppWorld, an agent benchmark, Bonsai leaps from 51.2 to 90.5, landing just behind the base model. On LiveCodeBench v6, the new version scores slightly lower than its predecessor.

On an RTX 4090, the model generates about 204 tokens per second using multi-token prediction. The weights are available under an Apache 2.0 license and run via llama.cpp on Nvidia and Intel GPUs, as well as through MLX on Mac, iPhone, and iPad. PrismML grew out of a research team at Caltech and is backed by Khosla Ventures, Google, and Samsung, among others. The company first introduced Bonsai 27B in July, built on an older Qwen model. Its smallest variant needed less than 4 GB of memory, small enough to run directly on an iPhone.

news.title: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Trump’s Demands to Another Chips CEO
news.title_en: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Trump’s Demands to Another Chips CEO
news.author: Noah Shachtman
news.summary_en:
The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms o
paragraphs: The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”

Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”

President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”

Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

“It's just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what's best for the company in the short or long term, what's best for shareholders, but what's best for politics and what the government is demanding.”

“That's not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you're talking about the world's most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that's a huge problem.”
Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

news.title_en: Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long
news.author: Aarian Marshall
news.summary_en:

paragraphs: In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

“Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.
“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.

paragraphs: One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history: cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food.

Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.

The group, which often goes by the online persona CyberAv3ngers, has a history of targeting critical infrastructure. In 2023 and 2024, it hacked Israeli-made industrial control devices inside water, manufacturing and transportation systems across several US states. Operational disruption was minimal, but the attackers left a message each time: “Every equipment ‘made in Israel’ is CyberAv3ngers legal target.”

State-backed Iranian hackers have rarely targeted Europe in this way, however. October’s hacks, experts say, mark an escalation in the Islamic republic’s cyber warfare strategy and a new willingness to hit European infrastructure.
“Iran has very clearly messaged that the global economy will be disrupted as a consequence of it being shut out from the world,” said Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations.

While France and other European countries have largely stayed out of the US and Israel’s campaign against Iran, which started in February, the Islamic republic increasingly views all Nato countries as legitimate targets, she continued. “This is about sowing panic in Europe and increasing that global pain threshold.”
Similar attacks were staged this month against supermarkets in 10 other countries across Europe, though no group has yet been blamed.

Iran has denied any role in the freezer hacks, but France is seeking international arrest warrants for three Iranians allegedly involved: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, believed by US intelligence to be head of the Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command, and two Shahid Kaveh leaders, 37-year-old Mahdi Lashgarian and 35-year-old Reza Salarvand. Both Lashgarians were placed under US sanctions in 2024.
Often staffed with young engineers and software developers, the Revolutionary Guards’ cyber units have developed formidable skills in espionage and cyber warfare.

“Iran is a country of engineers, and people continue to underestimate its capabilities,” said Sanam Vakil, Middle East director at Chatham House think-tank. “It has a long history of successful cyber operations,” she added, noting that Iran had learnt through its own experience of cyber attacks, most notably the Stuxnet assault on its nuclear programme by the US and Israel in 2009.

French intelligence agencies have said the group used a Chinese-made scanning tool to scour the public internet for connected refrigeration units. Infrastructure linked to the group also conducted reconnaissance using Modbus, a digital language widely used to control industrial machinery — a technique Shahid Kaveh has employed since at least April, according to the authorities.

Washington has spent years stopping advanced AI chips from physically reaching China. It turns out the chips never had to travel at all.

The rule comes from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS. It is an interim final
news.summary_en: The US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule, effective around November 16, 2026, targeting remote access to high-end AI compute by Chinese entities at non-US data centers. Facilities providing significant compute, exceeding 12 million aggregate TPP, are required to implement enhanced due diligence and obtain licenses, facing potential trade restrictions for non-compliance.
paragraphs: Washington has spent years stopping advanced AI chips from physically reaching China. It turns out the chips never had to travel at all.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department issued a rule aimed at Chinese companies that tap high-end AI hardware sitting in data centers outside China. The move lands hardest on Southeast Asia, a region that has been building server farms at a brisk clip.
The rule comes from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS. It is an interim final rule, with an effective date of approximately November 16, 2026.
Its core target is remote access. A Chinese firm does not need to own an Nvidia or AMD chip to use one. It can simply rent compute from a facility abroad and run its workloads over the internet.

The rule also reaches data centers directly. Any facility providing significant compute to Chinese entities needs a license and must carry out enhanced due diligence once it crosses a threshold of over 12 million aggregate TPP.
Operators get a 90-day compliance window after the rule takes effect. Those that miss it may face future restrictions.
There is one notable carve-out. US-headquartered operators are exempt from certain licensing requirements, though they must submit monthly compliance reports.

The rule is largely a response to the scandal around Nvidia and Megaspeed, a data center operator. Megaspeed spent at least $4.6 billion on Nvidia servers between 2023 and 2025.

The controversy centers on allegations that chips were diverted and that major Chinese clients, including Alibaba, gained remote access to compute. Those are allegations, not findings, but they were enough to push regulators into action.
Markets responded quickly. Shares of Southeast Asian companies linked to data centers fell after the announcement, with some dropping by as much as 20%.

news.summary_en: Researchers from MIT, ETH Zurich, and Imperial College London have developed a method to train AI climate emulators using synthetic data characterized by extreme environmental fluctuations, such as sudden CO2 spikes. This approach allows models to achieve high precision and robustness with only a single simulation run, significantly reducing computational demand.
paragraphs: MIT researchers have developed a method that makes training AI climate models faster, cheaper, and more reliable. According to MIT News, these emulators now need only a fraction of the data typically required.

Normally, researchers rely on massive, physics-based climate simulations that take months to run a single scenario on supercomputers. Fast AI models for climate prediction can mimic these in seconds and help plan power grids, public health measures, and agriculture. But training them previously required six to eight runs of those large simulations using evenly distributed, realistic future scenarios. That took so long the finished models were usually outdated, according to co-author Noelle Selin. They also often failed on unfamiliar situations.

An algorithm built by a team from MIT, ETH Zurich, and Imperial College London uses synthetic training data with extreme swings instead, like a sudden CO2 spike in 2050 or dropping methane in 2037. These targeted spikes help the AI understand the climate system far more precisely, according to lead author Christopher Womack. A single simulation run is enough for training, according to the team, and the AI reliably calculates the effects of local environmental policies too.

news.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues
news.title_en: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues
news.author: Sebastian Herrera
news.content_snippet:
Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter. Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how
news.summary_en: Meta Platforms and Amazon are negotiating the potential integration of Meta's Muse AI agent into Amazon's e-commerce platform, seeking to reverse a block imposed two months ago. The core tensions involve potential cannibalization of Amazon's advertising revenue and the risks of disintermediation between brands and their end consumers.
paragraphs: Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter. Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck. There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how exactly Muse would connect to Amazon. A major threat Muse poses to Amazon is that, in theory, it would bypass advertisements on Amazon’s website, which are a large source of revenue for the retailer.

Amazon is worried about losing advertising revenue and about the quality of the product search results Muse would surface, and executives are also concerned that shopping agents like Muse will weaken the relationship Amazon has with consumers, the people said. Any deal between Amazon and Meta is expected to require sign-off from the CEOs of both companies, they said.

Meta and Amazon declined to comment. The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents. As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers.

The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year. This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed.

AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries. Agentic shopping could total $190 billion to $385 billion in U.S. e-commerce spending by 2030, representing 10% to 20% of the total market, according to a 2025 report by Morgan Stanley. Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool.

Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements. Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and have autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars and booking reservations. As of October, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up the app, making it Meta’s biggest consumer AI hit to date. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case.

“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month in a call with analysts. “We’d like to create a large scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business. Advertising has become a $68.6 billion business for Amazon, representing nearly 10% of its total yearly revenue. In October, Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Still, Jassy said this month at a Semafor conference that Amazon hadn’t ruled out letting outside shopping agents into its store, but that they would have to provide a “fair exchange of value.”

Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent. Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.

Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before. In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps. Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases. The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.

news.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
news.title_en: AI is straining America’s open records systems
news.author: Rachel Courtland
news.content_snippet:
In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

news.summary_en: AI-powered automation is triggering a surge in public records requests across the U.S., forcing local agencies to handle significantly increased volume and scope. This influx has strained the limited resources of town and state offices, leading some jurisdictions to consider legislative changes to limit transparency requirements, potentially hindering open government.
paragraphs: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc .”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors. Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment. The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

news.author: Bloomberg
news.summary_en:
Walmart’s president and CEO Doug McMillon (left) with Flipkart co-founder Binny Bansal. The deal marks the latest milestone in Walmart’s drawn-out pursuit of India’s lucrative retail market Walmart Inc has signed definitive agreements to become the largest shareholder in the Flipkart Group, in a transaction that values Flipkart at $20.8 billion (around Rs 1.4 lakh crore).

The investment “underscores Walmart’s commitment to sustained job creation and investment in India, one of the largest and f
paragraphs: Walmart’s president and CEO Doug McMillon (left) with Flipkart co-founder Binny Bansal. The deal marks the latest milestone in Walmart’s drawn-out pursuit of India’s lucrative retail market Walmart Inc has signed definitive agreements to become the largest shareholder in the Flipkart Group, in a transaction that values Flipkart at $20.8 billion (around Rs 1.4 lakh crore).

The investment “underscores Walmart’s commitment to sustained job creation and investment in India, one of the largest and fastest-growing economies in the world,” the US company said in a press release on Wednesday.Subject to regulatory approval in India, Walmart will pay approximately $16 billion (around Rs 1 lakh crore) for an initial stake of approximately 77 percent in Flipkart, formally Flipkart Private Limited.

The remainder of the business will be held by some of Flipkart’s existing shareholders, including Flipkart co- founder Binny Bansal, Tencent Holdings Limited, Tiger Global Management LLC and Microsoft Corp, Walmart said in its press release. This implies that the other co-founder Sachin Bansal (unrelated to Binny Bansal) will sell all his stake in the ecommerce company he founded in 2007.

“India is one of the most attractive retail markets in the world, given its size and growth rate, and our investment is an opportunity to partner with the company that is leading the transformation of the ecommerce in the market,” Doug McMillon, Walmart’s president and chief executive officer, said in the press release.

India was a “critical market” for Walmart, he added. “Walmart has been looking to get into the Indian retail market for more than 15 years but the regulation of not allowing FDI into multi-brand retail has made it impossible for Walmart to access the Indian market,” Satish Meena, senior forecast analyst at consultancy Forrester, told Forbes India in an emailed statement.

“Walmart tried to enter via a wholesale model with Bharti Enterprises in India but failed. Now they see online as the only method to enter the Indian market, which leaves Flipkart as the best investment option for Walmart.”According to Forrester, the Indian online retail market was around $20 billion in 2017 (2.4 percent of total retail market in India).

No other market except China and US can compete in terms of total retail opportunity. Forrester projects the online retail market in India to reach $73 billion by 2022.In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2018, Flipkart recorded gross merchandise value(GMV) of $7.5 billion and net sales of $4.6 billion representing more than 50 percent year-over-year growth in both, according to the press release.

Currently, Walmart India operates 21 Best Price cash-and-carry stores and one fulfilment centre, across 19 cities in nine Indian states, with more than 95 percent of sourcing coming from India. In a presentation to investors, Walmart said that with Flipkart, there’s an opportunity to tap the latter's strong foundations in India, become the lowest cost operator and offer differentiated customer service.

The American company sees India as its only other “key growth market” apart from China, while America remains its core market, with a clutch of other markets comprising other growth opportunities — such as in Africa and Latin America. The Flipkart transaction is an exercise in marrying “local talent with global expertise,” Walmart said.Flipkart had 54 million active users in a market where there were 443 million millennials and about two-thirds of the country’s 1.3 billion population comprises the so-called ‘Generation Z’ or those who were typically born from the mid-1990s onwards.

India is also the second largest internet market in the world, by number of users — the first being China. India is also unique in that 79 percent of its internet users access the net via the mobile phone, whereas the proportion is about 50 percent for the global average.The company cited a report by consultancy Bain and Co. to point out it was entering a market where total retail is set to grow at about 9 percent whereas ecommerce is projected to surge ahead at a rate of 36 percent, growing four-times faster.

Penetration would triple from today’s 2.1 percent to 6.2 percent in the year 2023, therefore leaving a massive opportunity for further growth by achieving deeper online commerce penetration. Walmart and Flipkart are also in discussions with additional potential investors who may join the investment round, which could result in Walmart’s investment stake moving lower after the transaction is complete.

Even so, the company would retain clear majority ownership. Tencent and Tiger Global will continue on the Flipkart board, joined by new members from Walmart, according to the release.The final make-up of the board has yet to be determined, but it will also include independent members.

news.summary_en: The European Commission is pressuring adult platforms, including Pornhub, Stripchat, XNXX, and XVideos, to implement more robust age verification. This effort aligns with the development of a bloc-wide age verification application aimed at enhancing minor protection in the digital space.
news.title_zh: 欧盟拟向成人网站施压强化年龄核验
news.summary_zh: 欧盟委员会正督促Pornhub等成人网站引入更严格年龄核验，并筹备构建覆盖全欧盟的通用核验应用
paragraphs: Four large adult content websites are seeking to reach a deal with the European Commission on preventing children from accessing porn, as the sites try to minimise upcoming fines under the bloc’s push to protect minors online.

The Commission is investigating Pornhub, Stripchat, XNXX and XVideos for alleged breaches of the Digital Services Act by failing to adequately protect children from accessing adult content, as minors could access the porn platforms by simply claiming via one click that they are over 18. The DSA — which fully took effect in 2024 and forms part of the bloc’s broader digital rulebook — sets out how tech companies should police the internet.
The probe forms part of a broader European push to protect minors online that also includes a proposal to ban the use of social media, certain gaming platforms and AI chatbots by children under 13.

Since the start of the porn investigation in May last year, the four platforms have submitted co-ordinated commitments to address the concerns, but the Commission found those to be insufficient, two EU officials said.
The Commission is now discussing further remedies with the companies, although they are set to face fines for failing to take adequate measures in the past, the officials said.
Companies that fail to follow the EU digital rules face fines of up to 6 per cent of their global revenue, although the fines are rarely that high. The potential fines were first reported by MLex.

Brussels is simultaneously developing an EU-wide age-verification app that will allow all digital platforms, including porn websites, to confirm the age of a user without revealing additional personal information.

But it will take time to implement that technology, so the Commission is now discussing with the porn sites measures they can take to verify users’ ages in the transition phase. Any such measures would seek to avoid ongoing fines.
“We are looking into what we can accept,” one of the officials said.

The platforms have also raised concerns with the Commission that overly strict checks would lead adults to turn to lesser-known, smaller porn platforms which would be easier to access as they may have less strict age-verification systems.
To avoid this, EU member states have — in parallel with the EU probe — launched a co-ordinated crackdown on smaller platforms under national jurisdictions.
The companies did not immediately reply to a request for comment. The Commission declined to comment.

paragraphs: The boss of Amazon Autos believes there is plenty of room for more competition in the UK car advertising market as the retail giant prepares to take on Autotrader.

Speaking exclusively to Car Dealer in a video interview you can watch above, Matt Nuffort, director of Amazon Autos International, said he was undeterred by the number of established automotive marketplaces already operating in Britain.
Amazon has today confirmed it will launch its car advertising platform in the UK in early 2027, with Hyundai and listed dealer group Vertu among its first partners.
Asked directly by Car Dealer whether Autotrader should be worried about Amazon’s arrival, Nuffort said: ‘It’s a really large market and I think there’s a lot of room for many different competitors.’
However, he played down suggestions Amazon was targeting a particular position in the UK market.
Asked whether Amazon would be happy being a dominant number two or whether it was coming to Britain to be number one, he said: ‘We really don’t think in those terms.
‘We think in terms of, are we serving customers? And if we’re doing that, then I think we’ll be successful.’
Nuffort believes one of Amazon’s biggest advantages is the familiarity consumers already have with its technology.
‘We’re really offering Amazon technology, our digital storefront, to dealers to reach a wider set of customers,’ he said.
‘Customers often are already logged in. They already have the Amazon app. They’re familiar with the experience. Amazon Autos will look and feel like Amazon to them.’
While Amazon Autos will initially focus on franchised car dealers in the UK, Nuffort opened the door to independent used car dealers eventually being able to advertise their stock on the platform.
He revealed Amazon had already held talks with a number of businesses and trade associations.

news.author: Joe Miller, Alex Rogers, Ella Lee, Claire Jones, and George Hammond
news.content_snippet: Silicon Valley elites flexed their muscles in Washington to back Nvidia boss after humbling midterms defeat.
news.summary_en: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated after Silicon Valley investors, including Marc Andreessen, lobbied Vice President JD Vance and President Trump. Despite national security concerns raised by Secretary of State Marco Rubio regarding alleged spy ties, Trump prioritized the AI-led economic boom and tech market stability, supported by Attorney General Todd Blanche’s confirmation of no evidence of wrongdoing.
paragraphs: Silicon Valley’s alliance with Donald Trump’s White House looked broken this month, after voters punished Republicans and Big Tech donors, markets soured on AI and the boss of America’s biggest chipmaker went down in a spy scandal.

But in a single weekend, Trump’s tech allies reasserted their power in Washington, lobbying the commander-in-chief to defy his own intelligence agencies and lean on Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang as chief executive.
“The return of Jensen is the tech bros striking back,” said a former Trump official.
Tech investors, including Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner and Marc Andreessen, made entreaties on Huang’s behalf to officials including US vice-president JD Vance, who has deep ties to Silicon Valley.
Together they convinced the president that Huang was crucial to keeping the AI boom going, and Vance helped lobby Nvidia’s board to accept his return as CEO.
Silicon Valley figures proved they “still clearly have the president’s ear on these issues”, the person added.
However, Huang’s reinstatement could store up trouble for his allies in Trump’s orbit, since the Nvidia CEO still faces investigations that could unearth evidence that would tarnish his defenders.

Their victory came despite alarm among many Republicans about the national security implications of Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy. It was a setback for secretary of state Marco Rubio, who reportedly issued a memo to Trump officials warning of Huang’s close relationship with the woman.
Rubio, also Trump’s national security adviser, did not respond to a shouted request for comment during a brief appearance with the Qatari prime minister on Monday.

Trump was convinced to back Huang’s reinstatement by the plunge in tech stocks and warnings the US risked recession without Huang, which overrode security considerations, people familiar with the matter said.

Attorney-general Todd Blanche also assured the president that the Department of Justice had “no evidence of any wrongdoing by either Jensen Huang or Nvidia”, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Trump then repeated tech billionaires’ talking points about Huang’s singular importance to the economy in an hour-long TV interview with CNBC on Monday.

news.title_en: EU plans €50bn tech fund to close gap with US and China
news.author: Barbara Moens
news.summary_en:
The EU is drawing up plans to mobilise up to €50bn for a new fund that would make long-term, high-risk investments in European artificial intelligence and quantum computing companies, as Brussels seeks to reduce its dependence on US and Chinese technology.

The proposed Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (Stef) would make larger, riskier and longer-term investments than existing EU financing schemes, according to two officials involved in the discussions.

“These are long-term, stable investments in ris
paragraphs: The EU is drawing up plans to mobilise up to €50bn for a new fund that would make long-term, high-risk investments in European artificial intelligence and quantum computing companies, as Brussels seeks to reduce its dependence on US and Chinese technology.
The proposed Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (Stef) would make larger, riskier and longer-term investments than existing EU financing schemes, according to two officials involved in the discussions.
“These are long-term, stable investments in risky stuff,” one of the officials said. “It’s the opposite of what the EU usually does, which is exactly why we need it.”

The main focus of the investments will be in AI and quantum, which applies the principles of quantum mechanics to carry out calculations that are extremely difficult for conventional computers. The Commission will present a quantum strategy on Wednesday as it hopes to strengthen the bloc’s position in the emerging industry.
The new fund plans are part of a broader push to strengthen Europe’s technological independence amid growing uncertainty over US policy and an increasingly volatile geopolitical landscape.

Brussels also hopes to spur investment in emerging technologies where European companies have struggled to compete with their American and Chinese rivals. Stef investing in a company would encourage other investors to follow, the officials said.

Europe’s inability to fund and scale innovative tech companies is often cited as a key reason for the EU lagging behind the US and China, including in Mario Draghi’s recommendations on how to improve the bloc’s competitiveness.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen promised an “ambitious proposal” to finance initiatives aimed at bolstering the bloc’s “tech sovereignty” after a discussion among leaders on AI earlier this month.

The goal is set to present operational details of the new fund in February, the officials said, when EU leaders will discuss the bloc’s competitiveness at a retreat in the Belgian town of Alden Biesen.

The precise financing of the fund is still being discussed. The Commission aims to use EU funds as seed money that would attract additional investment from the private sector, with the aim to mobilise as much as €6 for every euro committed, one of the officials said.
EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen already discussed the fund idea with the European Investment Bank last week. The bank could provide financial expertise without carrying the investment risk itself.
Virkkunen said at a conference last week the fund should aim to attract €50bn, which is a 10th of what the Commission estimates it will cost to achieve full tech sovereignty.

news.title_en: How Meta is using Instagram to get an ad boost from its Muse personal AI agent
news.author: Julia Boorstin
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: Meta is integrating Instagram's user saving habits into its Muse personal AI agent to drive ad conversions. With 25% of Muse users engaged in shopping at an average transaction value exceeding $200, Meta has captured a 51% market share in agentic shopping, significantly outpacing Grok and ChatGPT.
paragraphs: Meta' s ad-free Muse personal artificial intelligence agent is already helping the social media giant boost its advertising business, and it's happening through Instagram, multiple people told CNBC.
Instagram is a major advertising revenue engine for the social media giant, and the company is leveraging existing habits on the platform by prompting users to organize their saved posts in Muse.

About 20% of daily Instagram users save at least one post to the app per day, according to a person familiar with the details, who asked not to be named because the information is not public. Many of those saved items, the person said, are either shoppable items or ads.

A senior executive told CNBC that Muse, even without ads, "is still very valuable for our ads business because it raises conversions for advertisers."It does this by reducing friction in the shopping process and allowing users to go back to items later, said the executive, who asked not to be named because the details have not been reported publicly.
"It gives advertisers a way to get more ROI for the dollars they're already spending, and that's all because Muse is helping people shop,"the executive said.

Mark Zuckerberg announced in Meta's last earnings call that 25% of Muse's users shop via the agentic tool — it's the most common use case for Muse — and the average purchase price is over $200. Zuckerberg said the company plans to take a small fee from transactions made through the agentic platform.

All that information about what people are shopping for with their agent is a valuable asset to target ads more precisely within Instagram. If consumers complete purchases with their Muse, that builds Meta's new revenue stream.
Meta's efforts to drive transactions seem to be paying off, and the buzz around Muse has made it a leader in agentic shopping.
In the week ending Nov. 22, 51% of all agentic orders were done by Meta's Muse, according to transactions measured by Forter Intelligence, an e-commerce analytics and cybertechnology company.

Meta dominates agentic AI shopping market share, according to Forter, which said that SpaceX 's Grok held a 24% market share in that same time period, followed by 22% to OpenAI's ChatGPT. The remaining 3% is divided between Google and startup Instinct.

Meta is expected to eventually launch ads in Muse, though multiple people said that it's not under any financial pressure to do so and tends to take its time building an audience before monetizing it.
The people said that putting ads in the Muse feed, which is more akin to a newsfeed instead of responses to specific queries, would be a natural way for Meta to test ads on the platform.

news.title: Officials Brief Congressional Staff on Intelligence Surrounding Nvidia Affair
news.title_en: Officials Brief Congressional Staff on Intelligence Surrounding Nvidia Affair

inline_images.caption: President Trump publicly proclaimed that Nvidia’s Jensen Huang was not a national security threat or facing criminal prosecution. (John Macdougall/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images)
inline_images.alt: President Trump publicly proclaimed that Nvidia’s Jensen Huang was not a national security threat or facing criminal prosecution.

news.author: Julian E. Barnes, Maggie Haberman, and Jonathan Swan
news.content_snippet:
A day after President Trump publicly proclaimed that Jensen Huang was not a national security threat or facing criminal prosecution, U.S. officials provided a tempered account of the intelligence at the heart of the Nvidia scandal in a briefing for Congress on Tuesday, people told about the briefing said.

The briefing, for staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees and aides to the leaders of both chambers, outlined in broad terms some of what intelligence agencies have colle
news.summary_en: Officials from the FBI, CIA, and ODNI briefed congressional intelligence committees on Alice Huang, who operated the Singapore-based Megaspeed firm suspected of diverting Nvidia AI chips to China. Intelligence indicates her ties to the Chinese Ministry of State Security, with her husband, Kang Wei, identified as a more significant intelligence asset. While high-level statements downplay criminal charges, Congress is demanding the release of the classified memo from Secretary of State Marco Rubio regarding these relationships.
paragraphs: A day after President Trump publicly proclaimed that Jensen Huang was not a national security threat or facing criminal prosecution, U.S. officials provided a tempered account of the intelligence at the heart of the Nvidia scandal in a briefing for Congress on Tuesday, people told about the briefing said.

The briefing, for staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees and aides to the leaders of both chambers, outlined in broad terms some of what intelligence agencies have collected on Alice Huang, the Chinese woman whose affair with the Nvidia chief is at the center of the episode.

The U.S. intelligence officials told the aides to the lawmakers that they still do not fully understand the role played by Ms. Huang, who helped to run a Singapore-based data center firm, Megaspeed, that is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence chips to China.

The briefers, who included officials from the F.B.I., C.I.A. and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, explained the contacts between Ms. Huang and China’s Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the meeting. The intelligence officials told the group there was no evidence she was directed by that agency to initiate an affair with Mr. Huang, though they did not dispute that she passed intelligence back to the agency after the affair began.

The briefers told the congressional staffers that the man who was often introduced as Ms. Huang’s husband, Kang Wei, was a more significant figure. He had been, at least at times, an M.S.S. asset and had more significant contacts with the Chinese spy agency, the briefers said.

The briefing did not include the most sensitive intelligence that the U.S. has collected about Ms. Huang, nor did it include a highly classified March 30 memo overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security adviser. That memo described Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang, and hers with Chinese intelligence services, according to people briefed on it.
The congressional intelligence committees have requested a copy of the Rubio memo.

The New York Times reported last month that the U.S. government had collected intelligence showing that Mr. Huang, an ally of Mr. Trump, was having a close relationship with Ms. Huang, who U.S. officials believed was an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The Times reported on Sunday that people briefed on the U.S. intelligence said Ms. Huang was in contact with the Chinese spy agency from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, covering at least part of the period when she was having the affair with Mr. Huang. The Times also reported that Mr. Kang was in contact with the spy agency, as well.

Soon after The Times first reported last month on Ms. Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence, Mr. Trump publicly suggested that he was unsure whether Ms. Huang was a spy, and declared Mr. Huang a good man and a genius deserving of support from the government. Over this past weekend, the president set in motion a drive by the White House to reinstate Mr. Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive, reversing the Nvidia board’s decision to force his resignation.

The company’s announcement Monday that Mr. Huang would return was quickly followed by a social media statement from Mr. Trump in which the president asserted that the Nvidia chief was not a security threat and that he was not a target of any criminal prosecution. Mr. Trump made those statements even though he was briefed at least twice about Ms. Huang’s ties to Chinese intelligence, including once by Mr. Rubio, The Times has reported, and even though the Justice Department investigation into the diversion of chips to China is still in an early stage.
The briefing on Tuesday for congressional aides continued, behind closed doors, the public pattern by the administration of seeking to minimize any damage to Mr. Huang and Nvidia from the episode.

news.title: Rajiv Ramaswami to step down as Nutanix begins hunt for its next CEO
news.title_en: Rajiv Ramaswami to step down as Nutanix begins hunt for its next CEO
news.author: Mike Wheatley
news.content_snippet:
Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.

In a letter to company employees, Ramaswami (pictured) said he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,”
news.summary_en: Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has announced his departure, triggering a leadership search and a transition period where he will serve as a senior advisor. Despite beating Q1 expectations with a 15% revenue increase, the company's conservative full-year guidance triggered an 8% drop in after-hours stock trading.
paragraphs: Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.

In a letter to company employees, Ramaswami (pictured) said he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,” he said in the letter.
Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.

“Our next CEO will inherit a strong platform, a loyal customer base and, most importantly, an exceptional team,” Ramaswami wrote. “Until then, my focus remains on leading this company and nothing about our day-to-day priorities changes. I am committed to helping our next leader succeed, and my ask of you, as always, is to continue to focus on executing as we go through this leadership transition.”

Ramaswami added that Nutanix has hired an executive search firm to lead the hunt for his successor. The news came as the company delivered its first-quarter earnings report, posting modest year-over-year gains in profit and revenue.

The company reported adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s target of 61 cents per share by a strong margin. Revenue for the period came to $772.4 million, up 15% from a year earlier and above the Street’s forecast of $762.7 million.

Nutanix’s outlook for the current quarter is strong, with the company guiding for sales of between $820 million and $830 million, compared with the Street’s consensus estimate of $820.4 million. However, the full-year picture is a little less rosy, with Nutanix guiding for annual sales of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion. The midpoint of that range trails the Street’s forecast of $3.22 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue.

Investors did not take the news very well. The cautious full-year guidance compared with the uncertainty over leadership prompted many to sell, and Nutanix’s stock was down 8% after-hours, having already fallen more than 5% during the regular trading session, on a down day for many tech stocks.

Virginia Gambale, of the board at Nutanix, hailed the “tremendous impact” Ramaswami had on the company during his six-year tenure. “Rajiv led the company’s transformation to subscription software, built a loyal and expanding global enterprise base and established a technology portfolio that we believe positions us well for the AI era,” she said. “We’re focused on selecting an exceptional leader who can build on that foundation.”
### A new chapter begins

In a conference call with analysts, Ramaswami said he believes the company is embarking on the third major chapter in its history. The first chapter, before his arrival, saw the company establish itself as the leader of the hyperconverged infrastructure industry. Chapter two began when he took over, and saw Nutanix expand from those roots to become a platform company, he said.

“[We have] transformed the company to be profitable while growing and expanding the product portfolio quite significantly, from HCI to a platform that works across clouds, supports external storage and has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future with AI capabilities,” Ramaswami said. “Chapter two is well-established at this point and there’s a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth. I feel like we are in a very good place.”

paragraphs: HP GAVE a profit forecast for the current year that will likely exceed analysts’ estimates, signalling the computer and printer maker is improving its ability to manage rising costs associated with memory chips. The shares jumped in extended trading.

Earnings, excluding items such as restructuring costs, will be US$3.15 to US$3.45 a share for the year beginning this month, the company said on Tuesday (Nov 24) in a statement. Analysts, on average, projected US$3.18, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

For the current quarter ending January, profit will be 66 cents to 76 cents a share, HP said. Analysts, on average, estimated 72 cents. The forecasts include the impact of tariff refunds, the company said.
The shares rose about 15 per cent in late trading after closing at US$27.94 in New York. The stock had gained 15 per cent this year through the close.
HP and other computing device makers are coping with an unprecedented surge in demand for memory chips fuelled by the AI build-out.

Amid skyrocketing costs for those components, HP has raised prices on its products, leading consumers to push off buying new computers. Corporate customers, however, are investing in new machines and revenue in that business rose 23 per cent.
Sustainability has reached Apac boardrooms but are board members sufficiently equipped? Find out more in our report.
Global PC shipments declined more than 22 per cent in the July-September period from a year earlier, according to industry research firm Gartner.

“We continued to grow our higher-value businesses, with AI PCs reaching nearly 60 per cent of shipments, while taking steps to address memory and storage cost pressures,” Bruce Broussard, the company’s interim chief executive officer, said in the statement.
Revenue increased 9.3 per cent to US$16 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, which ended Oct 31. Profit, excluding some items, was 83 cents a share.

Analysts, on average, estimated earnings of 74 cents on revenue of US$15.3 billion. The earnings included a larger-than-forecast tariff refund of 15 cents a share, compared with a previously forecast 8 cents.

“While our fiscal 2027 outlook reflects a prudent view of continued cost and demand pressures, we have a strong track record of addressing challenges and are confident in our ability to drive improvement in our profitability throughout the year,” said chief financial officer Karen Parkhill.

news.content_snippet:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.

The news comes hours after The New York Times reported that the Central I
news.summary_en: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) of the U.S. Treasury has confirmed unauthorized access to a subset of its systems and initiated an investigation. FinCEN, responsible for anti-money laundering, has taken systems offline as a precaution while maintaining reporting channels via hotline.
paragraphs: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.

The news comes hours after The New York Times reported that the Central Intelligence Agency and Office of the Director of National Security discovered a breach of an open source intelligence system, exposing unclassified information. It’s unclear if the FinCEN breach is related. Americans have been on high alert about security incidents after a series of seemingly unrelated outages earlier this month.
"Americans have been on high alert about security incidents"

FinCEN’s role is to protect the financial system from illegal activity, including by combatting money laundering and terrorism financing. The bureau maintains financial transaction data and distributes it for law enforcement purposes. FinCEN also houses reports of suspicious activity that financial institutions file as part of the Bank Secrecy Act.

FinCEN says in its alert that banks can still file reports about suspicious activity online, but some services may not be immediately available. Filers that need to expedite their reports in the meantime can still call the Financial Institutions Hotline, which it says was not impacted by the disruption.
